## Start with a specific question

**LeetCode 315 — Count of Smaller Numbers After Self.** We will reason from a very small example rather than introduce a complicated notation first.

## What the obvious approach overlooks

Try every pair to count how many later numbers are smaller; this is quadratic for long arrays.

## One simple idea

Mathematical counting turns a yes/no predicate into a 0/1 contribution. Then an appropriate data structure can aggregate those contributions without revisiting all later values.

Before reading symbols, explain the intended operation aloud. If you can say which information is saved and which work is avoided, you have the core intuition.

## Formula and immediate translation

$$
C_i=\sum_{j=i+1}^{n-1}[\,a_j<a_i\,]
$$

**Symbols and notation:** C_i is the number of entries after index i strictly smaller than a_i; n is total length; [condition] is 1 when true and 0 otherwise.

**Insert actual numbers:** For [5,2,6,1], C₀ counts later values smaller than 5: 2 and 1 qualify but 6 does not, so C₀=1+0+1=2. C₁=1 (only 1 is smaller than 2), C₂=1, C₃=0.

This numerical calculation is essential: the expression must mean the same thing when evaluated by hand and when written in code.

## Why the mathematics leads to an algorithm

Every pair (i,j) with i<j contributes exactly once when the later value is smaller. Summation of indicators produces the desired count without ambiguity.

This argument is the bridge between 'the equation looks plausible' and 'the result is correct for all inputs satisfying the assumptions'.

## Make the idea executable

The [original algorithm examples](../examples/patterns.mjs) provide a small runnable related operation:

~~~js
import { mergeSort } from '../examples/patterns.mjs';

console.log(mergeSort([5,2,6,1]));
~~~

Run from a saved `.mjs` file inside this topic directory. The exported operation is tested with Node's standard test runner. Some examples illustrate a prerequisite rather than the entire specialised algorithm; in that case, the mathematical model above remains the definition of the full task.

## Complexity and correctness boundaries

**Work bound:** O(n²) direct counting, O(n log n) with divide-and-conquer or Fenwick tree; n is array length.

**Counterexample or limitation:** This counting definition is NOT itself a fast algorithm: using nested loops still costs O(n²). Merge sort or Fenwick trees can evaluate all counts in O(n log n).

Always declare the input domain first. For example, a modulus must be positive, a probability denominator nonzero and a character indexing convention fixed. Many seemingly clever solutions fail because these conditions were never stated.
